facts.claim: A study of 15 excessive users of violent games and control subjects showed no differences in brain responses when viewing pictures of emotional and neutral situations.
facts.quote: While the typical pattern of activations for empathy and theory of mind networks was seen, both groups showed no differences in brain responses.

facts.claim: A longitudinal fMRI study on non-gamers found no evidence for desensitization in the empathy network for pain in the violent video game group at any time point.
facts.quote: We did not find any evidence for desensitization in the empathy network for pain in the violent video game group at any time point.

facts.claim: The perception of others' pain were not significantly different in brain regions between groups of participants with and without long-time exposure to violent video games.
facts.quote: The results showed that the perception of others' pain were not significantly different in brain regions between groups, from which we could infer that the desensitization effect of VVGs was overrated.

facts.claim: Professional experience seems to desensitize physicians to the pain of others without necessarily helping them down-regulate their own personal distress.
facts.quote: Professional experience seems to desensitize physicians to the pain of others without necessarily helping them down-regulate their own personal distress.

research.angle: While professional experience is linked to desensitization to the pain of others, research on violent video games consistently fails to find evidence of neural desensitization in empathy.
research.verdict: The evidence contradicts the idea that violent media causes neural desensitization, though professional exposure to suffering is associated with a desensitized perception of pain.
research.caveat: The study on physicians is observational and shows an association rather than a proven cause for desensitization.
